name: 30-second chair stand
summary: How many times you can stand up fully from a chair and sit back down in 30 seconds, without using your arms. It reflects leg strength and endurance. More is better.
howTo: Use a firm chair without arms, seat about 43 cm high (the height used in the Polish norms; the Colombian study used 43–46 cm), with its back against a wall. Write down the height and use the same chair next time.
Sit in the middle of the seat, feet flat on the floor about shoulder-width apart, arms crossed over your chest.
On 'Go', stand up fully (hips and knees straight), then sit all the way down. Repeat as many times as you can in 30 seconds. Arms stay crossed.
Count each full stand. If you are more than halfway up when the 30 seconds end, count it as one (the Senior Fitness Test convention, as described by Lein 2022).
Do it once, or once after a short practice; write down which, and do it the same way next time.
safety: Do it with someone nearby, the chair against a wall, and nothing around you to trip over.
Skip it, or ask a physiotherapist first, if you have recently had hip or knee surgery, sharp joint pain, dizziness on standing, or have been told to avoid exertion.
Stop at once if you feel dizzy, short of breath, chest pain or joint pain.
Wear flat, non-slip shoes or go barefoot on a non-slip floor.

norms.label: Poland (60+)

source.title: Functional fitness normative values for elderly polish population

norms.population: 5,367 adults aged 60–93 (4,164 women, 1,203 men) living independently in six regions of Poland; recruited through senior centres, public institutions and media adverts (volunteers, although the authors call the sample representative). Ethics approval 2015.
norms.note: Oldest participant 93. Mean ± SD per band are also in Table 1 (e.g. women 60–64: 15.7 ± 4.3; men 60–64: 16.1 ± 5.4). Men are under-represented (22%), and the men's 85+ band has only 36 people.

norms.label: Colombia (18–80)

source.title: Reference values for sit-to-stand tests in Colombian adults: a multicenter cross-sectional study

norms.population: 393 self-reported healthy adults 18–80 (208 women, 185 men) recruited through social media, e-mail and word of mouth in four Colombian cities, 2023–2024; BMI over 35 excluded; some had controlled hypertension or diabetes.
norms.note: The only open-access source found with 30-s norms by sex across 18–80. Groups are small (24–57), so the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles rest on one or two people. Colombian 60–69 medians (13 women, 15 men) are a little below the Polish 60–64/65–69 medians (15, 16). Keys p2_5 / p97_5 = 2.5th / 97.5th percentile. Small groups (about 25 to 60 people each), so only the middle percentiles are shown; the paper's group counts don't add up to its totals.

evidence.claim: Slower chair rising is linked to higher death rates in older adults, but the studies timed five rises; for the 30-second count the link is only indirect.
whyThisGrade: The pooled evidence (5 cohorts, 28,036 people, hazard ratio 1.96 slowest vs fastest quarter) used a timed five-rise test, not a 30-second count
The two tests are closely related (r = −0.79 between them in young adults, Lein 2022) but not interchangeable
Observational, high heterogeneity (I² 81.9%), mostly people over 70
No study linking the 30-second count itself to mortality was verified for this file

studies.title: Objectively measured physical capability levels and mortality: systematic review and meta-analysis
Normative Reference Values and Validity for the 30-Second Chair-Stand Test in Healthy Young Adults

limits: The count depends on chair height, whether you practised, how many tries you had, whether half-stands count, and tiredness from earlier tests. Young-adult results ranged from a median of about 20 (Colombia, single trial) to a mean of 33 (US students, best of two after practice).
Open norms for ages 20–59 come from one small study (393 people in Colombia). Treat percentiles under 60 as rough.
It mixes leg strength, endurance, balance, joint pain and effort. It can't tell you which one limits you.
A low count doesn't diagnose anything, and no study found here shows that raising your count changes your health risk.
